Payment rails: types, examples and a global list

By the Ibanora teamPublished November 25, 202610 min read

In short

Payment rails, also called banking rails, are the systems that clear and settle money between banks and other payment providers. Examples include ACH and Fedwire in the US, SEPA in Europe, Faster Payments and CHAPS in the UK, Lynx and the Real-Time Rail in Canada, UAEFTS and Aani in the UAE, and the card networks. SWIFT carries payment messages, and the money itself settles through accounts that banks hold and through domestic systems.

Payment rails are the systems that move money between banks and other payment providers. Each rail has an operator and its own rules. Common examples are ACH and Fedwire in the US, SEPA credit transfers in Europe, Faster Payments and CHAPS in the UK, and the card networks. SWIFT is often listed with them, but Swift describes itself as a messaging network: it carries payment instructions, and the money settles through banks' accounts and domestic systems.

What are payment rails? Banking rails explained

People also call them banking rails. Every rail does two jobs. Clearing is the exchange and checking of payment instructions between providers. Settlement is the transfer of money between the providers' accounts that completes the payment. The Federal Reserve describes both steps for its ACH service: the Reserve Banks receive files of payments from the sending banks, sort them and deliver them to the receiving banks, then settle them by crediting and debiting the banks' settlement accounts.

Rails differ in what they settle with. Some settle in central bank money, meaning accounts that banks hold at the central bank. The European Central Bank says T2 settles payments this way, with no upper or lower limit on their value. The Central Bank of the UAE says its UAEFTS moves funds between banks through their accounts at the central bank and settles each transfer individually, without netting debits against credits.

Other rails are run by private companies. The Clearing House describes CHIPS as a private-sector system for high-value US dollar payments. It continuously matches and offsets payments between participants, so they need less funding than they would if every payment settled on its own.

Types of payment rails

Most rails fall into one of six groups:

  • Batch and next-day rails carry payments such as payroll and direct debits on business days. The Federal Reserve says banks send each other batches of ACH payments, Payments Canada calls its ACSS a retail batch system, and the UK's Bacs handles Direct Debits and Direct Credits. Under the EU's Payment Services Directive, the payer's provider must make sure a euro transfer reaches the payee's provider by the end of the next business day after it receives the order, or two business days for a paper order.
  • High-value rails, often called wire systems, carry large or time-critical payments. Fedwire, CHAPS, T2 and Lynx settle each payment individually as it arrives, a model called real-time gross settlement (RTGS). The UAE's UAEFTS is also an RTGS system, and CHIPS settles high-value payments by offsetting them.
  • Real-time rails run around the clock: FedNow and RTP in the US, SCT Inst in Europe, Faster Payments in the UK, the Real-Time Rail in Canada and Aani in the UAE.
  • Card networks route card payments between the merchant's acquirer and the bank or other company that issued the card.
  • Correspondent banking moves money across borders through accounts that banks hold with each other, with instructions sent over SWIFT.
  • Blockchains and stablecoins are an emerging group, covered further down.

Is SWIFT a payment rail?

Not in the same sense as the rails in the table. Swift says it does not move money. It calls itself a secure messaging system that helps financial institutions send payment instructions, while the funds move through banks, fintechs and other institutions. Swift also says it is not a bank: it is a cooperative, and its community is made up of banks, fintechs, financial institutions and companies.

The money in a cross-border bank payment moves through correspondent banking. In its 2016 report, the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) calls correspondent banking an essential part of the global payment system, especially for cross-border transactions. It defines it as an arrangement in which one bank, the correspondent, holds deposits owned by other banks, the respondents, and provides payment and other services to them. Its role in domestic payments has shrunk greatly because those now run through financial market infrastructures. For US dollars, The Clearing House says CHIPS clears and settles domestic and cross-border wires, including correspondent banking payments.

Two domestic rails show the split between messaging and settlement. The Bank of England settles each CHAPS payment individually in its RTGS system, and CHAPS direct participants must have access to the SWIFT network. In Canada, Payments Canada owns and operates Lynx, and Swift is the message service provider whose network carries the participants' payment instructions.

ACH payment rails and real-time rails compared

ACH is the main US batch rail. Nacha governs the network, and two operators process the payments: the Federal Reserve and The Clearing House. Nacha estimates that 80% of ACH payments, credits and debits together, settle in one banking day or less.

According to Nacha, the ACH network is open 23¼ hours every business day and settles payments four times a day. Settlement depends on the Federal Reserve's settlement service, which is closed on weekends and federal holidays, and from 6:30 p.m. to 7:30 a.m. ET on business days. Same Day ACH has a $1 million limit per payment, which Nacha says rises to $10 million on September 17, 2027.

The Federal Reserve says the FedNow Service went live on July 20, 2023 and has a 24-hour business day every day, including weekends and holidays. As of November 2026, The Clearing House says its RTP network runs 24/7/365 and takes payments of up to $10 million each.

A payment can only use a real-time rail if both banks have joined it. FedNow is available to depository institutions in the United States, and The Clearing House publishes lists of RTP participants and of routing numbers that can receive RTP payments. For the details a US payer needs to send money to an account, see IBAN vs routing number.

Card payment rails

The Federal Reserve's Regulation II, in 12 CFR 235.2, defines a payment card network as an entity that provides the services, infrastructure and software that route information from an acquirer to an issuer to carry out the authorization, clearance and settlement of debit card transactions. The acquirer is the party that settles card payments for the merchant, and the issuer is the party that authorizes the use of the card.

US rules also give each debit card a choice of networks. The Federal Reserve says Regulation II stops issuers and networks from limiting debit transactions to fewer than two unaffiliated networks. It also stops them from preventing a merchant from routing a debit transaction over any network the issuer has enabled.

Crypto payment rails: blockchains and stablecoins

Public blockchains can also move value between parties. Stablecoins are tokens on them that aim to hold a steady value against a currency; our guide what is a stablecoin explains how they work. In its 2025 Annual Economic Report, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) says stablecoins were designed as a gateway to crypto, promising a stable value against currencies, overwhelmingly the US dollar, while running on public blockchains. It names their uses as on- and off-ramps for crypto and, more recently, cross-border payments for people in emerging market economies who lack access to dollars.

The BIS then tests stablecoins against three requirements for the core of a monetary system, and finds they fall short on all three:

  • Singleness: money should be accepted at full value with no questions asked. Stablecoins carry the name of their issuer and often trade at varying exchange rates.
  • Elasticity: the system should supply enough money for large payments to settle without gridlock. Stablecoins are typically backed by an equal amount of assets, and each new coin needs full payment upfront, which the BIS calls a cash-in-advance constraint.
  • Integrity: the system should resist financial crime. The BIS says stablecoins are bearer instruments on borderless public blockchains, which has made them a go-to choice for illicit use, and that the lack of know-your-customer standards like those of the traditional financial system adds to the problem.

The CPMI and the Financial Stability Board have also set out conditions. In an October 2023 report, the CPMI said no stablecoin arrangement yet existed that was deemed to be properly designed and regulated and fully compliant with all relevant regulatory requirements. It added that any benefits for cross-border payments must not come at the cost of the principle of "same business, same risks or risk profile, same regulatory outcome". The Financial Stability Board's July 2023 recommendations ask authorities to regulate, supervise and oversee global stablecoin arrangements and to require clear governance and risk management. The BIS report says tokenized platforms with central bank reserves, commercial bank money and government bonds at the center can lay the groundwork for the next monetary and financial system.

What decides which rail a payment uses

Several conditions limit which rails can carry a given payment:

  • Currency and location. Most rails in the table handle one currency, so a payment that changes currency or country needs a route between rails, such as correspondent banking.
  • Amount. As of November 2026, Faster Payments takes up to £1m, Same Day ACH up to $1 million and RTP up to $10 million per payment, while CHAPS and T2 have no upper limit.
  • Timing. On a weekend, the rails in the table that run 24/7 stay open. On business days, the Federal Reserve sets a 6:45 p.m. ET deadline for Fedwire transfers on behalf of a bank's customer, and the Bank of England says CHAPS customer payments must be submitted by 5.40pm.
  • Participation. Both providers must belong to the rail, directly or through another institution. Payments Canada says the Real-Time Rail is targeted to serve over nine in 10 Canadian bank accounts by the third quarter of 2027.

Questions

What is the $3,000 bank rule?

A $3,000 threshold appears in the US funds "travel" rule. FinCEN guidance says the rule applies to transmittals of funds of $3,000 or more, or the foreign equivalent, but not to transfers governed by the Electronic Fund Transfer Act (Regulation E) or made through ATM or point-of-sale systems. For a covered transfer, the sender's financial institution must pass on details such as the sender's name and address, the amount, the date and the recipient's financial institution, and intermediary institutions must pass that information along.

Is XRP a payment rail?

XRP is the cryptocurrency supported by the XRP Ledger, which xrpl.org describes as a decentralized blockchain that uses its own digital currency to process and record financial transactions. The ledger is the network that moves value, so it fits the broad idea of a crypto payment rail, and XRP is the asset on it. Unlike the rails in the table, it has no single central authority: validator servers agree on each new version of the ledger.

How many payment rails are there?

There is no fixed number, because each country runs its own systems, and card networks and blockchains add more. For bank payments in the US alone there are ACH, Fedwire, CHIPS, FedNow and RTP, plus the card networks.

Can one payment use more than one rail?

Yes. A SWIFT transfer sends its instructions over Swift and moves the money through correspondent banks and systems such as CHIPS. In Europe, TIPS settles real-time euro payments and is built to comply with the SCT Inst scheme. In Canada, Interac said at the Real-Time Rail's launch that Interac e-Transfer payments were beginning to clear and settle on the new rail.
